title: How Long Does Foundation Underpinning Take in San Francisco? A Real Timeline
metaTitle: Foundation Underpinning Timeline in SF (2026) | Real Week-by-Week Schedule
excerpt: Foundation underpinning in San Francisco typically takes 6–16 weeks from engineering to final inspection — but the timeline splits into 5 phases most contractors don't explain. Here's what to actually expect.
primaryKeyword: how long does foundation underpinning take
proposalRationale: Fills a foundation-cluster gap. outline.h2: The Short Answer: SF Foundation Underpinning Takes 6–16 Weeks
outline.notes: Direct answer up top. 6–8 weeks for straightforward helical pier projects on accessible sites. 10–16 weeks for push piers on Victorians or complex sites requiring extensive engineering. Slabjacking: 1–3 days actual work but 2–4 weeks including scheduling. Breakdown coming.

outline.h2: Phase 1: Engineering and Assessment (2–5 Weeks)
outline.notes: Structural engineer site visit, soil analysis if required, load calculations, pier design, stamped plans. Cost embedded: $3K–$8K. Marina fill and bay mud add soil boring requirements. Note this phase is often skipped by cheap bidders — a red flag.

outline.h2: Phase 2: SF DBI Permit and Plan Review (3–8 Weeks)
outline.notes: SF Department of Building Inspection (DBI) plan review. Standard review 3–5 weeks; over-the-counter possible for simple projects; complex projects with Structural Advisory Committee review can hit 8+ weeks. Marin CDA and Oakland Planning & Building Department run similar timelines. Historic districts add 2–4 weeks. Permit fees: $2K–$5K.

outline.h2: Phase 3: Site Prep and Mobilization (3–5 Days)
outline.notes: Utility locates (USA 811 — 2 business days minimum), protection of existing finishes, dust barriers, equipment staging, potentially neighbor notification for shared property lines. On steep SF streets, staging alone can take an extra day.

outline.h2: Phase 4: Underpinning Installation (1–4 Weeks by Method)
h3: Helical Piers: 1–2 weeks for typical 8–16 pier project
outline.notes: Each method's actual installation duration. Helical: 4–6 piers per day typical. Push piers slower because of counterforce requirements. Slabjacking fast because no excavation. Weather delays: winter rain adds 3–7 days average.

outline.h2: Phase 5: DBI Inspection and Sign-Off (1–3 Weeks)
outline.notes: Rough inspection during installation (per-pier or per-day depending on inspector), final inspection after backfill and cleanup. DBI inspection scheduling: 2–5 business days lead time typical. Note that engineered fill and compaction testing may add a day. Certificate of Final Completion closes out the permit.

outline.h2: What Extends the Timeline
outline.notes: Bulleted list with specific delay ranges: bay mud requiring extended pier depths (+3–7 days), historic district review (+2–4 weeks), Structural Advisory Committee review (+4–6 weeks), utility conflicts discovered mid-dig (+3–10 days), winter rain (+3–7 days), neighboring property access negotiations (+1–4 weeks).

outline.h2: Real SF Underpinning Timelines (Three Actual Projects)
outline.notes: Three concrete project examples with real week counts. Marina 12-pier helical: 9 weeks total. Alamo Square Victorian push pier 14-pier: 15 weeks total. Bernal Heights garage slabjacking: 3 weeks total. Each broken down phase by phase.

outline.h2: The Short Answer: Yes, in Most Bay Area Cities
outline.notes: Direct answer. Any deck over 30 inches above grade requires a permit in nearly every Bay Area jurisdiction — a threshold set by California Residential Code (CRC) Section R105.2. Ground-level platforms under 30 inches, under 200 sq ft, and detached from the house are usually exempt. Everything else = permit.

outline.h2: Why Do Bay Area Cities Require Deck Permits?
outline.notes: Question-form H2. Three reasons: structural safety (attachment to house, guardrail loads), seismic (Bay Area zone 4), and code compliance (fire, egress in WUI zones). Deck collapse case history is real — cite it. Not a bureaucratic annoyance.

outline.h2: San Francisco DBI Deck Permit Requirements
outline.notes: SF-specific. DBI plan review, over-the-counter for simple decks under specific thresholds, structural engineer stamp required for multi-level and hillside decks. Note historic district review adds 2–4 weeks. Actual permit fees itemized.

outline.h2: Marin County Deck Permits (Mill Valley, Sausalito, Tiburon, Kentfield)
outline.notes: Marin CDA handles unincorporated areas; each incorporated city (Mill Valley, Sausalito, Tiburon, San Rafael, Ross) has its own department. WUI zones require Class A fire-rated materials — affects deck board choice. Slope-hazard review common.

outline.h2: East Bay Deck Permits (Oakland, Berkeley, Piedmont)
outline.notes: Oakland and Berkeley both handle deck permits in-house. Oakland Hills WUI zone adds ember-resistant requirements. Berkeley Landmarks Preservation Commission (LPC) may apply in landmark districts.

outline.h2: Peninsula Deck Permits (Palo Alto, Menlo Park, Burlingame, San Mateo, Daly City)
outline.notes: Each Peninsula city runs its own building department. Palo Alto is notoriously slow (6–12 weeks). Menlo Park moderate (4–8 weeks). Daly City Department of Economic & Community Development moderate. All follow the 30-inch rule.

outline.h2: What Happens If You Build Without a Permit
outline.notes: Real consequences: DBI/CDA can issue stop-work orders, require tear-down and rebuild to code, impose fines ($500–$5,000+ typical), block property sale disclosures, void homeowner insurance claims on deck failures. The 'nobody will find out' myth — building departments do drive-bys, neighbors report, sale disclosures trigger audits.
